cause: A component of the ammonia heating element failed causing a reduction in the flow of ammonia to the SCR. Ammonia in sufficient quantity is necessary to convert NOx to N2 and water. When this reduced ammonia supply occurs the lbs/hr. NOx increases. Upon further investigation, it was determined that an electrical relay switch had developed an electrical short circuit which prevented some of the ammonia from being heated and distributed to the selective catalytic reduction (SCR) for NOx abatement.
actions: We reduced the load of carbon black being produced in order to accommodate the reduced ammonia available to treat the NOx emissions. The damaged electrical relay was replaced and the ammonia treatment to the SCR was restored. The entire ammonia injection system had to be shut down in order to complete the electrical relay repair.

cause: The Maintenance event was for 36 hours but the Opacity event only happened during the shutdown of the ESP and last for just a few minutes. The FCCU was taken offline to allow for the installation of an engineered clamp on the reactor/regenerator pipe flange. The clamp was attempted to be installed while the unit was in normal operation but the temperatures of the equipment was too hot. The contractor hired has special high temp PPE to do jobs like this but at 1300 degrees it was too hot for the duration that was needed to complete the installation. As a result we had to lower the FCCU to minimum rate and put it on circulation. That then lowered the temperature of the equipment to 800 degrees. Since it was on circulation there was no flue gas exiting the FCCU so the CO Boiler, SCR, ESP were bypassed. The ESP being shut down is what causes the Opacity.
actions: In order to ensure the safe shutdown of the ESP, the TR sets are required to be turned off before shutting down the flue gas to the unit. This is required because if the TR Sets stay on while pulling flue gas feed to the ESP oxygen would be introduced into the ESP and cause an explosion. This shutdown process is to ensure safe operations.

cause: After the severe winter weather Texas experienced in mid-February, the EVGP was shut down from lack of field gas. Upon restart of the plant, the sulfur recovery unit (SRU) was left down for inspection and associated repairs from the freezing conditions. Initial gas rates into the plant produced very little acid gas, but as the plant returned to pre-severe winter weather conditions, the flaring of acid gas reached reportable levels. Flaring was intermittent for 130 hours and 4 minutes during a 136 hour time period.
actions: Various water piping leaks and equipment damage were found. Repair work began immediately but took several days. Sour gas into the site was minimized in order to reduce the SO2 emissions generated from the flaring of acid gas. Flaring ended once all repairs were completed, the system was verified to be working properly and the SRU was restarted. The acid gas flare was maintained in constant operation, flare pilots were continuously monitored and no bypassing of the control device occurred.
basis: Flaring emissions based upon metered gas volume, gas analysis and event duration. Calculations based upon TCEQ guidance document known as RG-109.

cause: The #2 SCOT lost quench flow circulation on the quench tower due to sulfur buildup which caused the Amine section of the unit to pressure up and trip the burner on the mixing chamber. The loss of the mixing chamber took the SCOT unit off line, leaving just the SRU section of the plant running. In this operation mode the unit has a destruction rate of 95% instead of 99% going into the incinerator. Once the tower was cleared and the circulation restored the unit was returned to operation.
actions: Operational moves were made immediately to minimized emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with standard operating procedures and good pollution control practices and implemented sulfur shedding procedures.

cause: Due to the possible increased volume of liquid from the Poly DGA Stripper OH Cooler and the cooler not being service during the event allowed liquids to stay entrained in vapor to the Carlile Pot. As a result, there was hydrocarbon carryover from the Carlile Pot to the #1SRU KO Pot and increased the level. However, we do not believe this was a true liquid level but a hydrocarbon gas due to the extra reactor exotherm. This ended up causing low O2 levels in the Muffle Furnace and the flame loss. When the furnace flame is lost it is designed to relive the unit to its control device (North Flare). The flame was quickly reestablished, the Muffle Furnace was brought on line and the valve to the flare was closed within ~20 minutes.
actions: Operational moves were made immediately to minimize emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with standard operating procedures and good pollution control practices. Implemented sulfur shedding procedures and restarted the unit as quickly as possible. We called out Maintenance, fixed the fire eye, and the unit returned to normal operations as quickly as possible. We are performing a full Root Cause Failure Analysis (RCFA) as required by NSPS Subpart Ja and our EPA Consent Decree.

cause: The main belt on DHT Off gas compressor broke and tripped the compressor offline. This resulted in the compressor relieving to the North Flare. The belt over time will build up slack, when the belt gets slacked it will slip on the pulley creating heat. As the belt was heated up, it stretched more, slipped more and overheated until it broke. This belt was replaced a month ago during the February freeze thawing period. After the installation, the belt is adjusted as need within the first couple of weeks to account for the initial stretching and heating. Historically, once that initial period of adjustments the belt is secure and will operate without issue for a long period of time.

Implemented Off Gas minimization and cut-rate on contributing units. Maintenance followed up daily to check on the new belt and adjusted it as needed until no further adjusment was required and the belt is broken in. also, as part of operaterator rounds there is a sound and heat check to monitor the belts safe operation.

cause: A mystery stream of H2S showed up in the North Flare. During this time all process units associated with the affected flare were operating as designed. Operations started their search of the source using the Flare Management Plan (FMP) and along with flare header sampling. Operations was draining the liquid from the SRU knock-out drum through the DGA knock-out drum to the flare. The operator had drained all of the contents out of the SRU knock-out drum and had closed the 2” block valve to the suction side of the pump. The line between the SRU Knock-out drum and the pump contains a 2” and a 3” block valve. Shortly after this occurred, the flare experienced high levels of H2S. Operations check multiple options to find the source of the high H2S and rechecked the 2” block valve from the SRU knock-out drum at least two times. During the last search for the source of the high H2S, operations closed the 3” block valve from the SRU knock-out drum and the H2S concentration immediately started to decrease.
actions: Operations moved to investigate not only using our Flare Management Plan (FMP) but also performed an evaluation of abnormalities in process limits and normal operations. We executed our enhanced H2S investigation process which includes flare header sampling (please note that the north side has 4 headers that tie into the main header with multiple possible contributors of H2S to the flare) to identify the unknown source. After the source was found the plan to prevent recurrance is:*The operations/maintenance will have the 2” block replaced/repaired*The operations procedure for draining the SRU knock-out drum will be modified to include closing both the 2” and 3” block valves after the drum has been drained *A low level alarm will be installed/added that will notify the board operator when the level in the SRU knock-out drum goes below a set level. The will help to insure that the water seal in the drum is maintained and operations has an indicator that the block valves may be leaking and allowing the drum to drain out.

facility: HOWARD GLASCOCK SOUR GAS INJECTION FACILITY
cause: This was an unforeseen and unscheduled emergency flaring event which was caused as a result of the need to purge nitrogen from the system after the need to pig the gas gathering line. Flaring started on 10/20/2021 at 18:00 hours and ceased on 10/21/2021 at 8:00 hours when the gathering line purging was completed for a total duration of 14 hours. This event was considered reportable due to the exceedance of the SO2 threshold as a result of this emergency flaring. The Howard Glasscock Field and the AGI Plant were purchased from ConocoPhillips in late 2017. The AGI Plant was designed by ConocoPhillips to sweeten the natural gas produced by the Howard Glasscock Field prior to sales. A simplistic description of the AGI Plant processing is asfollows: 1. Gather associated sour natural gas produced from the Howard Glasscock Field; 2. Pressure the gas at the inlet for processing and sales (Inlet Gas Compressor); 3. Remove and concentrate the H2S and CO2 from the natural gas prior to sales (Amine Unit); 4. Inject the H2S and CO2 in the Doris Cole 14D UIC Injection Well (Sour Gas Compressor); 5. Remove the moisture from the sweet natural gas prior to sales (Glycol Dehydration); 6. Flare used as a control for process stream emissions and MSS; 7. Flare also used as a control for emergency situations and scheduled maintenance Depending on the circumstances at the AGI Plant, different process streams may be sent to the flare during a particular emissions event. These typical excess emission event streams include the following: • Inlet Field Gas @ 60,000 ppm H2S • Off Spec Gas @ 50 ppm H2S • Sales Gas @ 0 ppm H2S • Plant ESD (Scheduled) @ 0 ppm H2S • Plant ESD (Non-Scheduled @ 94,000 ppm H2S • Acid Gas @ 450,000 ppm H2S. For this emergency flaring event, field gas (60,000 ppm H2S) was flared as part of the Facility startup operations during the purging of the nitrogen from the system. Note that the AGI Plant Permit by Rule (PBR) includes provisions for MSS; however, no credit has been taken to-date in our excess emissions reporting and none is taken in this response.
actions: As described above, the purpose of the AGI Plant is to remove H2S and CO2 from the raw natural gas stream coming into the facility so that sweet gas can be sold. The removed H2S and CO2 are then concentrated, pressured, and then injected in the Doris Cole 14D underground injection control disposal well. Although the purpose of the amine unit at the plant is to remove H2S and CO2 to minimize emissions of these pollutants to the atmosphere, the amine unit is not considered pollution control equipment under the facility air permit as there are no direct emissions from this equipment – the removed H2S and CO2 are injected underground. The flare serves as the permitted control device in the air permit and as a control during emergency situations and MSS operations. The flare operation includes streams from the glycol dehydrator still vent, startup operations, shut down operations, upset conditions, and emergency situations. This flaring event was considered an emergency situation. The flare stack operated as designed for this emergency flaring event and converted the H2S to SO2 in a safe manner. Note that there are no public areas within at least a 1 mile radius of the AGI Plant. Flaring is an accepted oil and gas industry practice for safely handling gas releases. Startup operations resulted in the flaring of field gas after the purging of the nitrogen from the system was completed and the system could be returned to sales. The purging of the gathering line was completed so quickly as soon as possible. Citation personnel executed practicable measures to minimize emissions. No pollution control equipment was bypassed. The emissions were minimized by flaring the gas,which is assumed to have a 98% destruction efficiency for H2S and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). The duration of the event was minimized by having the plant operator respond immediately to the event and with startup operations beginning as soon as the purging of nitrogen was completed. All emission monitoring systems operated as designed. Operators documented the event and actions and advised the person responsible (Director EHS/Regulatory) for emissions events reporting. Applicable reporting was made in a timely manner once it was determined that a reportable quantity would be exceeded. The emissions were not part of a frequent or recurring pattern. There are no residents or public areas within at least a 1 mile radius of the AGI Plant. The facility is remote with restricted access to the public. No complaints were received, and no modeling or monitoring was performed.
basis: Production rates combined with site specific analytical data and engineering estimates.

cause: The side wall of the Unit 2 Primary Bag Filter (PBF) broke away allowing carbon black to escape through the side of the building. cause: The instrument air supplying the North side process units froze up due to condensate build up in the air system. cause: The FCCU has 3 air blowers. All 3 blowers are needed for the full operation of the Fluid Cat Cracking Unit (FCCU). For this event the #2 Blower tripped Offline on motor over current from high air flow. The motor Distributed Control System (DCS) overload controller was design to reduce air flow to lower the load on the blower. There was a "Soft Stop" set on this controller's output at 25%. This prevents the controller from reducing the air flow past this point. As the air flow was not being reduce and the air density increased with the drop in temperature causing the motor load (amps) to cross the over current blower curve's threshold and tripped the blower. This triggered the emergency shut down of the FCCU and started a cascade of events. The loss of air flow cause low delta pressure (DP) across the regenerator slide valve which results in the Cat feed to be diverted away from the unit and guarantees the shutdown of the Cat Cracker unit. This resulted in exceeding the Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) 500 lbs. / 24 hr. Reportable Quantity (RQ).
actions: Moves were made to quickly and safely bring the FCCU down and secure safe operation of downstream units. The unit stayed down until the initial investigation was completed in order to understand the cause and fix needed it to make sure that when the unit came back up we did not have the same equipment issue happen again. The investigation showed that the #2 blower suction valve actuator had a lot of hysteresis (slop) as it reverses from moving open to close or closed to open and valve positioner was not reading the correct valve position feedback and was not controlling the valve to the commanded position. This created a 15% error throughout the control range. Another item identified in the investigation was that the valve's actuator had a significant pneumatic leak around the rod seal which is not able to be see or check externally of the suction valve. After understanding why, the blower tripped offline, the blower suction valve was repaired. A new electronic positioner was purchased and installed. A rebuild kit for the actuator was purchased and installed (a new one was going to be week before we could get it). All parts were driven via Hotshot arrived the next day. The #2 blower suction valve was re-assembled and tested to ensure the valve was for fit for service and turned over to Operations allowing the safe startup and operation of the FCCU. The Operational moves made were to minimize emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with operating procedures and good pollution control practices.
basis: Emissions in this event include the emergency shutdown of the FCCU and the start up after equipment repairs. Also they are based on process knowledge, flows and material balances, best engineering judgment, CEMS monitoring data, and engineering calculations.

cause: The #1 SRU had an electronic failure of the Programable Logic Controls (PLC) processor which shut down the whole unit. The PLC recorded an error that required it to a stop condition because it could no longer solve the logic. At this point all the PLC control safety variables (i.e., Valves, Blowers, Pumps) were placed in their designed fail-safe state…This function closed the acid gas inlet valve (feed to unit) to the SRU which in turn open the pressure control valve to the flare and resulted in exceeding the Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) 500 lbs./24 hr. Reportable Quantity (RQ).
actions: Operations immediately increased flow to #2 SRU to allow the #1 SRU Acid Gas feed to be diverted to #2 SRU and away from the flare. At the same time, they started implementing the Sulfur shedding procedure to eliminate the remaining acid gas flaring. The PLC processor manufacture instructions for the error code stated that it can be reset by power cycling the processor. The processor was power cycled, and the card returned to normal operations. An additional card was ordered and Hot Shotted - driven straight to the refinery from the vendor and was schedule to arrive the next morning. Shortly after the reset, the PLC processor failed again, so the unit remained down until the additional purchased processor arrived the next morning. It was installed and the unit has operated without issue since that time. All moves were made immediately to minimize emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with standard operating procedures and good pollution control practices.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on process knowledge, flows and material balances, best engineering judgment, CEMS monitoring data, and/or engineering calculations. The duration of the event includes some residual or lingering emissions after the unit was closed off to the flare and had to roll off before getting back close to baseline.

As a result, there was a loss of electrical power in the Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) portion of the Refinery affecting the main boiler feed water pumps. This caused the boiler feed water supply to not be fed to the CO Boiler and it triggered an automatic shutdown. This resulted in the FCCU flue gas being diverted through the CO Boiler Bypass Stack with the steam loss being made up by other steam providers.
actions: Operations immediately cut charge rate to the FCCU and increased temperatures to achieve full burn in the FCCU. Unit, safety systems shutdown the Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) Transformer/Rectifier (T/R) Sets diverting flue gas to the CO Bypass Stack. The CO Boiler stayed down until it cooled down enough to reignite the burner and reintroduce flue gas to the combustion zone (the CO Boiler normally operates at 2600 degrees and must cool down to below 700 degrees before you can add fuel gas to ignite the burners otherwise, it would be unsafe. This affects the duration required to be in the bypass stack. Once the flue gas was reintroduced to the CO Boiler, the ESP T/R Sets were reenergized and diverted the flue gas back into the ESP. All other process units were stabilized and/or operated at reduced rates to support the FCCU operating at reduced rates while in full burn mode.

cause: The #1 SRU had an electronic failure of the flame scanners that monitors the presence of the flame in the muffle furnace. The flame scanners on the muffle furnace began reading erratically, each going in and out of alarm for approximately 5 minutes. The erratic behavior of the scanners culminated with both being in alarm caused the unit to shut down, this is a designed fail-safe state. This function closed the acid gas inlet valve (unit feed) to the SRU which in turn opened the pressure control valve to the flare and resulting in exceeding the Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) 500lb/24 hr. Reportable Quantity.
actions: Operations immediately decreased flow to #2 SRU to allow the #1 SRU Acid Gas feed to be diverted and transferred to #2 SRU and away from the flare. At the same time, they implemented the Sulfur shedding procedure to eliminate the remaining acid gas flaring and reduce the amount of acid gas being processed by the SRUs. Instrumentation and Electronic Technician (I&E) performed trouble shoot techniques using circuit drawings for the main control panel to navigate through hundreds of wires to determine a cause. The investigation found that the wiring with both flame scanners were compromised. One was a loose wire for the top flame scanner which was re-inserted/resecured and the other one was a loose terminal on the bottom flame scanner which was also resecured. Once electrical systems were certified good operations implemented the startup procedures. All moves were made immediately to minimize emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with standard operating procedures and good pollution control practices.

cause: The Fuel Gas Treater (FGT) Stripper acid gas flow started acting erratic and was subsequently adding above normal liquid level to its downstream knock out pot. This pot is designed to knock out liquid from the off-gas stream before it goes to treatment. An investigation determine that the Cat Light Ends (CLE) unit was having operational pressure swings causing liquid carry over to the FGT, as a result the FGT stripper bottom pumps were tripping offline causing an upset in downstream flow to its knockout pot which routes the FGT off gas to #1 SRU. As operations worked to understand the process upset conditions and stabilize the units, the FGT upset flow was carrying liquid and surges of off gas to the #1 SRU. As a result, # 1 SRU is not designed to handle feed surges much less with liquid and therefore the unit tripped offline closing the acid gas inlet valve (feed to the unit) and opened the pressure control to the flare, as designed for safety, resulting in exceeding the Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) 500lbs/ 24hr. Reportable Quantity (RQ). These conditions were intermittent over several days. The first impact causing an SO2 flaring event occurred on 5/28/2022; however, investigation, trouble shooting, and issue resolution transpired over several days to not only identify the cause, but also the resolution to the cause. This resulted in additional intermittently flaring and process upset activities over the event time of ~100 hours.
actions: Key pressure, temperature, level instruments and gauges were checked to ensure proper operation. The FGT stripper OH level was not reading correct, and its controller tunning parameters were off spec. The Amine section of the FGT was found to have been contaminated with oil and required to be drained and replaced with fresh. A pump on the CLE tripped offline and required repair. The FGT and Flare knock out pot had to be drained of free liquid. Addressing and fixing these items were a combination of maintenance craft being called out to the plant for the prompt investigation and repair, vendors suppling fresh Amine to the Refinery, and Operators purging lines and clearing equipment. This was a multi-discipline and multi-day response to return the units back to normal operations. During this time operational moves were made to minimize emissions and were aggressive to the best extent possible in a manner that is consistent with safe operating procedures and good pollution control practices and all affected process units were stabilized as soon as practical.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on CEMS data, process knowledge, flow and material balances, best engineering judgment, and/or calculations.

cause: The reformer overhead condensers were not cooling as required due to external fouling around the tubes causing light end hydrocarbons containing sulfur compounds to get carried into the excess hydrogen going to the reformer flare. The concentration of the reduced sulfurs and the vent flow in the header resulted in exceeding the 500 pounds per 24-hour Reportable Quantity limit.
actions: An investigation and research were performed on unit process operations for any abnormal conditions to determine cause of event. Above normal temperature was noticed on the Reformer effluent fin fan cooler, which was affecting normal operation and the quality of the excess hydrogen going to flare as explained in the cause of the event above. Operations initially cut rate to reduce flare flow from the Reformer process unit and to also lower the fin fan cooler temperature. Operations immediately started cleaning the fin fan cooler with a fire hose to remove the external scale, this started to bring the temperature down even more. These two activities restored the normal operating temperature which stopped the condensing of light end hydrocarbons containing sulfur compounds being carried into the flare system. In addition, a 3rd party performed a chemical cleaning of the whole external cooler surface to ensure long-term proper performance of the cooler.

cause: The FCCU CO boiler had a temperature indicator fail and start reading flatline data. This flatline temperature reading caused the water seal drum to evacuate its seal triggered by the Safety Instrumentation System (SIS). The CO boiler combustion temperature controller process variable input stopped responding, resulting in the fuel gas pressure control valve slowly closing. Because the combustion temperature controller was still providing a process variable that was not accurately reflecting the process conditions, the combustion temperature continued to decrease. This temperature decreased to the "trip threshold". It resulted in the water seal drum evacuation and the FCC flue gas effluent being diverted to the FCC bypass stack to prevent lower explosion limit (LEL) levels of CO and excess oxygen from entering the electrostatic precipitator (ESP) that could have resulted in an explosion. This resulted in exceeding the 5000lb/24hr CO Reportable Quantity (RQ).
actions: Operations and instrumentation technicians quickly investigated this evacuation of the water seal drum and identified the bad process variable indicator. Once this was identified as the contributing factor to the activation of the early trip, the console operators switched the temperature indication that was being used to control the combustion temperature to the backup, which provided an accurate reading. This allowed the operators to increase the combustion zone temperature enabling the trip alarm to clear, and reintroducing the FCC flue gas into the CO boiler.

cause: During a thunderstorm, the CO boiler tripped due to a loss of boiler feed water; the loss of feed water was the result of the boiler feed water pumps tripping offline. The loss of boiler feed water triggered the safety instrumentation system (SIS), releasing the Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) water seal drum and diverting the FCCU flue gas to the CO boiler bypass stack. The diversion of the flue gas to the bypass stack resulted in exceeding the CO 5000lb/24hr, SO2 500lb/24hr, and 35% Visible Emissions (VE) Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits.
actions: Operations immediately cut the charge rate to the FCCU and increased temperatures to achieve full burn in the FCCU. Unit safety systems shut down the Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) Transformer/Rectifier (T/R) Sets, diverting flue gas to the CO Bypass Stack. The CO Boiler is required to cool down enough to reignite the burner and reintroduce flue gas to the combustion zone. This takes several hours because the CO Boiler normally operates at >2600 degrees and must cool down to below 700 degrees before allowing fuel gas to ignite the burners; otherwise, it would be unsafe and potentially cause an explosion. This directly affects the duration required to be in the bypass stack. However, the FCCU will reach full burn (which means full destruction of CO) ~12 hours. Once the flue gas was reintroduced to the CO Boiler, the ESP T/R Sets were reenergized and diverted the flue gas back into the ESP. All other process units were stabilized and/or operated at reduced rates to support the FCCU operating at reduced rates while in full burn mode.Instrumentation and Electrical technicians were called to investigate the cause and restore power to the boiler feed water pumps. During the I&E investigation, the technicians found a blown lightning arrestor on the main power feed line to the boiler feed water pumps. The lightning arrestor was replaced, the power substation was reset, and the boiler feed water pumps were restarted.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on CEMS and COMS data, process knowledge, flow, material balances, and best engineering judgment.

cause: During normal operations of the Fluidized Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU), the steam turbine main air blower governor became stuck in the minimum position. At the same time, the unit was on circulation, maintenance was executed, and repairs were completed on the CO Boiler before returning the FCCU to full operation. This repair took several days to complete under the authorization of our Maintenance, Startup, Shutdown (MSS) permit, which extended the time of the event. This activity was discussed with Region 7 to inform them of the refinery status.

process_units: FCCU Bypass Stack; FCCU ESP Stack
cause: During a thunderstorm, the 5-1 Feeder, high voltage electrical feed, had a phase-to-phase short, resulting in the boiler feed water pump tripping offline; operations started the steam-driven boiler feed water pump, but it would not stay running due to the motor over speeding and the safety system forcing it to shut down. As a result of the boiler feed water pumps shutdowns, the CO boiler tripped on a loss of feed water, which triggered the safety instrumentation system (SIS), releasing the Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) water seal drum and diverting the FCCU flue gas to the CO boiler bypass stack. The diversion of the flue gas to the bypass stack resulted in exceeding the CO 5000lb/24hr, SO2 500lb/24hr, and 35% Visible Emissions (VE) Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits.
actions: Operations immediately cut the charge rate to the FCCU and moved to increased temperatures to achieve full burn in the FCCU. Unit safety systems shut down the Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) Transformer/Rectifier (T/R) Sets, diverting flue gas to the CO Bypass Stack. The CO Boiler is required to cool down enough to reignite the burner and reintroduce flue gas to the combustion zone. This takes several hours because the CO Boiler normally operates at >2600 degrees and must cool down to below 700 degrees before allowing fuel gas to ignite the burners; otherwise, it would be unsafe and potentially cause an explosion. This directly affects the duration required to be in the bypass stack. However, the FCCU will reach full burn (which means full destruction of CO) ~12 hours. Once the flue gas was reintroduced to the CO Boiler, the ESP T/R Sets were reenergized and diverted the flue gas back into the ESP. All other process units were stabilized and/or operated at reduced rates to support the FCCU operating at reduced rates while in full burn mode.Instrumentation and Electrical technicians were called to investigate the cause and restore power to the boiler feed water pumps. During the I&E investigation, the technicians found a blown fuse on the main power feed line to the boiler feed water pumps. The fuse was replaced, the power substation was reset, and the boiler feed water pumps were restarted.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on process knowledge, flows and material balances, best engineering judgment, CEMS monitoring data, and/or engineering calculations.

cause: The January Polar Vortex severe cold event impacted the operation of several units within the refinery. The first unit affected was the #2 Sulfur Recovery Unit (SRU). The #2 SRU developed a plug in the quench section of the Shell Claus Off-Gas Treating (SCOT) unit; in an attempt to melt the plug, tail gas was required to be routed around the SCOT and directly into the quench section, then venting through the incinerator. The crude charge heater lost temperature, resulting in the charge to the crude tower losing temperature, preventing the crude charge from being able to circulate in the tower and plugging up the crude tower. This caused the refinery to move into a controlled shutdown. Along with the shutdown, the refinery experienced ruptured piping, equipment malfunctions, process upsets, and unit gasses being routed to the appropriate flare. Please note that emissions were intermittent throughout this freeze event, as well as plant maintenance, recovery, and refinery shutdown/startup. There were days without excess emissions going to a flare and days when only one or another flare was in excess. The event's duration was from when the first unit went down and exceeded the 500 lbs./ 24-hour reportable quantity until all refinery units were up and stabilized (January 14, 2024, through February 7, 2024).
actions: Before the winter freeze began the refinery was set at stable reduced rates. When the #2 SRU triggered the first emission event the refinery activated the sulfur shedding procedures and shifted load over to #1 SRU. The refinery was forced to stay running at stable reduced rates until the freezing period was over to prevent further damage and emissions. After this period, the refinery moved into shutdown in preparation for maintenance and scheduled repairs to be completed before bringing the refinery back online. Maintenance was performed around the clock during this outage to ensure a quick response to impacted equipment and to minimize emissions. Please note that throughout the freeze event, thaw period, and refinery shutdown, maintenance and operations rescued equipment problems and potential malfunctions due to the round-the-clock support.

cause: The Brooking Compressor Station and many other WTG facilities in the North Permian System have been receiving historically high levels of oxygen ("O2") from third-party producers, and due to the sheer number of contributing 02 source(s) the ability to pinpoint the sources and isolate the contaminant could not be achieved. Furthermore, because WTG's compressors are equipped with O2 shut down set points (to protect process equipment to prevent equipment damage and safety hazards) and because the O2 levels where excessively high, the entire WTG North Permian field experienced continuous flow interruptions causing the O2 to further contaminate the system. Additionally, high O2 levels forced downstream markets not to be able to accept WTG processed gas, which would also be harmful to the long-term integrity of the pipeline system. The issue was further compounded by the winter weather, where compressors that were shut down due to the high O2 levels would then freeze up resulting in further spread of the O2 throughout the system.
actions: After diligently searching for and unsuccessfully identifying the contributing O2 sources that began in the middle of December 2023, WTG made the decision to purge the north Permian Basin field of all gas currently in the system and flush the system with new gas to eliminate the high O2 gas. Additionally, WTG installed 13 permanent new O2 analyzers strategically in the gathering system and used approximately 23 portable O2 analyzers in an effort to pinpoint the third-party source(s) of the O2. WTG also sent notice to all its producers regarding the problematic O2 levels and requesting the third-party producers to investigate, correct, and prevent O2 leaks into the system. When O2 was discovered above the parts per million (ppm) threshold, WTG would shut in the producer well battery. Starting at 9:00 am on January 25, 2025, Brooking Compressor Station was shut down and all incoming pipelines from the third-party producers were purged to remove the damaging O2 concentrations, and this continued until the O2 sensors determined that O2 levels were safe and had returned to on-specification levels. All purged gas was directed to flare, which was in constant operation during the event, and flare pilots were monitored, and no bypassing of the control device occurred. This O2 purge was part of a system-wide purging event in the entire WTG North Permian System. On January 30, 2025, O2 levels were back to reasonable specification and the Brooking Compressor Station was restarted. Since this time, while there are intermittent O2 spikes that still occur, the ability to quickly identify, isolate and respond to the O2 excursions has been successful. WTG has ordered 75 additional O2 analyzers and plans to permanently install these throughout the WTG system to isolate and prevent further system wide contamination recurrence. Additionally, WTG is communicating with third-party producers and requiring adherence to and enforcement of the concentration specifications requirements.

cause: The CO boiler was scheduled for maintenance to perform a routine water wash on the superheater section to clear sodium fouling in the boiler tubes in May 2024, requiring the boiler to be taken offline and bypassed. cause: Due to a refinery steam system upset, steam shedding procedure was enacted; as a part of the steam shedding procedure, the CO Boiler circulation pump was switched from a steam-driven turbine to an electrical pump. Once the steam system was recovered, the CO Boiler switched back to the steam turbine circulation pump and returned the electric pump back to standby. Immediately after this swap, the steam turbine governor tripped on overspeed. The circulation pump tripping caused the Safety Instrumentation Systems (SIS) to shut the CO Boiler down, resulting in exceeding the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for carbon monoxide (CO), Opacity and Sulfur Dioxide (SO2).
actions: Operations immediately reduced the charge rate to the Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) and elevated temperatures in the regenerator tower to ensure complete combustion of CO (full burn) within the FCCU. As a safety measure, the unit's safety systems shut down the Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) Transformer/Rectifier (T/R) Sets, redirecting flue gas to the FCCU Bypass Stack. Subsequently, the CO Boiler needed to undergo a cooling process to enable burner reignition and reintroduction of flue gas into the combustion zone. The CO Boiler normally operates at temperatures exceeding 2600 degrees and it must cool down to below 700 degrees to safely ignite the burners, preventing the potential for explosion. This cooling phase typically lasts several hours. Consequently, this process directly impacts the duration required to remain in the bypass stack. Upon reintroduction of flue gas into the CO Boiler, the ESP T/R Sets were reactivated, redirecting flue gas back into the ESP. Additionally, all other process units were either stabilized to support the FCCU's operation at reduced rates during full burn mode.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on CEMS and COMS data, process knowledge, flow, material balances, and best engineering judgment.

cause: During severe weather, a lightning strike occurred at the 10-11 substation. This tripped off the 5-3 electrical feeder, causing DCS (Distributed Control Systems) outages and interruptions. This high-voltage feeder provides electrical for the FCCU parts of the HDS-Reformer unit and the Tank Farm. With the loss of the CO Boiler, the FCCU regenerator section immediately vented to the bypass stack, while the Wet Gas Compressor loss forced the venting of the FCCU reactor section to the South Flare. The venting through the FCCU bypass and South Flare exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) for CO and SO2 (5000 lbs./24 hrs. and 500 lbs./24 hrs., respectively).

This I&E investigation determined a fusible link within a breaker on the 5-1 feeder broke, as designed, during a power surge (lightning strike), and prevented the breaker from resetting. Once repaired, it was safe to restart the affected equipment.

process_units: Diesel Hydrotreater; No. 1 Sulfur Recovery Unit; No. 2 Sulfur Recovery Unit
cause: At approximately 9:57am, the Refinery Northside primary control system had a circuit board failure that caused the several process units to divert to the north flare. This resulted in exceeding the SO2 500lb/24hr Reportable Quantity limit.All Control valves on that circuit board automatically reverted to fail-safe mode, which is the manual position for the valves. The control valves affected were the No. 1 Sulfur Recovery Units (SRU) acid gas dump valve, the acid gas charge (feed) valve for both No. 1 and No. 2 SRUs, the Diesel Hydrotreater (DHT) charge drum pressure controller. These activities cause No. 1 SRU to shut down and required unit temperatures to cool to minimum before restarted and affected the duration of the event. In addition, No. 2 SRU could not receive feed gas from No. 1 SRU because the feed valve was frozen at 17%. Recovery from this upset was complex.
actions: Operations implemented the sulfur shedding procedures and quickly moved to reduce unit rates across the refinery. Process Controls and Instrumentation and Electrical (I&E) technicians performed troubleshooting procedures to determine the system failures while Operations moved to stabilized multiple process units. This investigation determined that a DCS card had malfunctioned, resulting in the valves moving to the failsafe position. I&E replaced the DCS card and returned the unit to operations. Operations returned units to normal operations.

process_units: Fuel Gas Treater; Hydrogen Desulfurization Unit (HDS); Reformer Unit; Saturated Light Ends; Vent Gas Compressor
cause: During normal operations, the Saturated Light Ends (SLE) feed charge pump failed, leading to a plant-wide disruption due to the SLE's connections with upstream and downstream units. Consequently, the upset in the SLE affected the Hydrogen Desulfurization Unit (HDS) and Reformer units. This upset resulted in exceeding the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limit of 500 lb./24 hr. of SO2 at the north and crude flares, while the Reformer and South flares experienced Subpart Ja H2S exceedances (>162ppm 3hr avg).
actions: The failure of the pump caused the SLE feed charge to be diverted to the North flare. Operations redirected the SLE feed to the Fuel Gas Treater (FGT) header to reduce emissions from the North flare. This action over-pressured the Vent Gas Compressor (VGC), causing its discharge to back out of the FGT header and trip the VGC, diverting its feed gas to the Crude flare. The diversion of the SLE charge to the FGT also over-pressured the fuel gas contactor, leading to venting at the South flare. Concurrently, operations reduced the refinery crude feed and the feed to the hydrotreaters to stabilize the units and the refinery. This redirection strategy resulted in fewer emissions compared to leaving the SLE feed charge in the North flare.

cause: While at reduced operating rate for maintenance on the number 3 air blower, the Fluidized Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) tripped offline due to the number 1 blower shutting down without warning. The number 1 blower shut down due to a lube oil pump failure caused by a plugged wye strainer on the steam line feeding the drive steam to the lube oil pump. This resulted in the FCCU flue gas being diverted to the CO Boiler bypass stack and the FCCU reactor section venting to the south flare. This event exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for 500lb/24hr SO2 at the South flare and CO Boiler bypass stack and CO 5000lb/24hr at the CO Boiler bypass stack.
actions: Operations stabilized the FCCU by putting the reactor section in circulation and halting the charge to the FCCU. Upon finding the wye strainer on the steam line plugged, it was cleaned, and the lube oil system was inspected for any other failure indications. Following the inspection, operations put the number 1 blower back online and restarted the CO Boiler. This allowed the FCCU regenerator section to reenter the CO Boiler and unit charge resumed in the FCCU.

cause: While at reduced operating rate for refinery inventory requirements, the Fluidized Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) tripped offline due to the number 1 and number 3 blowers shutting down and the reactor and regenerator sections showing erratic differential pressures. Upon investigation, the cause for these issues was an instrument air supply line that was plugged with ice formation. This resulted in the FCCU flue gas being diverted to the CO Boiler bypass stack and the FCCU reactor section venting to the south flare. This event exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for 500lb/24hr SO2 at the South flare and CO Boiler bypass stack and CO 5000lb/24hr at the CO Boiler bypass stack. During this event, one of the two refinery Natural Gas supply lines (from 3rd party sources) was shutdown coming into the refinery. This disrupted all refinery heater operations, which in turn led to upset conditions in the Crude, Reformer, North-side Hydrotreaters along with delaying the recovery of the FCCU and CO Boiler. This led to Crude, Reformer, and North flares being impacted, but these did not exceed RQ limits for SO2.
actions: Operations stabilized the FCCU by putting the reactor section in circulation and halting the charge to the FCCU. Upon finding the instrument air supply line plugged, the ice plug was melted and condensation in the system was drained. An inspection of the overall system followed allowing operations to put both blowers online. The CO Boiler was shut down and had cooled, which led to requiring extended time to recover from the event. In addition, recovery of natural gas to heaters (including FCCU/CO Boiler) also delayed the recovery of refinery operations, which added to the total time of the event.
basis: Emissions reflected in this report are based on CEMS data, process knowledge, flow, material balance, best engineering judgment, and/or calculations.

cause: Alon USA, LP - Big Spring Refinery (BSR) required catalyst changes in both the Reformer unit and Diesel Hydrotreater (DHT) unit that began in early February. As these two units operate with critical inputs from upstream processes and have Hydrogen gas as a critical process gas, all upstream and downstream units were correspondingly reduced in rate with emissions occurring at the Crude, Reformer, Northeast, and South flare. During this maintenance outage, the refinery experienced extremely low ambient temperatures that caused maintenance actions on units that were not originally identified in the initial STEERS notification. These are the FCCU (#1 Blower), 24 Boiler (tubes), and waste gas treating areas (exchanger repair) and were included for the successful completion of the maintenance outage. This resulted in the FCCU flue gas being diverted to the CO Boiler bypass stack and the FCCU reactor section venting to the South flare. This event exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for 500lb/24hr SO2 at the Reformer, North, and South flare and CO 5000lb/24hr at the CO Boiler bypass stack.
actions: Operations stabilized upstream and downstream process units during the shutdown, catalyst changes, and startup of the Reformer and DHT units. During the repair of the FCCU #1 Blower (shaft and bearing repairs), the FCCU reactor section vented to the flare while the unit was put in circulation and halted the charge to the FCCU. The CO Boiler was shut down and had cooled, which led to requiring extended time to recover from the event. In addition, recovery from the loss of 24 Boiler required further delays and extended the repair/maintenance scheduled timeline.

cause: While awaiting completion of repairs to #24 Boiler (600#-steam boiler) at Alon USA, LP - Big Spring Refinery (BSR), the other operating 600#-steam boiler (#23 Boiler) suffered an unexpected and sudden shutdown. This led to the Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) #1 and #3 Blowers (steam-driven) shutting down and caused the FCCU to shut down. This resulted in the safety system activating the FCCU flue gas diversion to the CO Boiler bypass stack and the FCCU reactor section venting to the South flare. This event exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for CO 5000 lb/24hr and SO2 500 lb/24hr coming from the regenerator to the CO Boiler bypass stack.
actions: Operations stabilized the FCCU by stopping charge and shuttering downstream process units immediately during the boiler shutdown and loss of all 600# steam. Within hours of the loss of #23 Boiler, the #24 Boiler had completed repairs and became operational. Maintenance personnel began assessing the FCCU #1 Blower and found major damage requiring an extended repair period, while the #3 Blower was found operational. With adequate steam now available, but #1 Blower not operating, it was decided to operate the FCCU matching the available air supply and having the flue gas re-introduced to the CO Boiler. During the investigation and start of #24 Boiler, the FCCU reactor section vented to the flare while the unit was put in circulation and halted the charge to the FCCU. The time required to start #24 Boiler and determine FCCU operational status led to extended time needed to recover from the event.

cause: During routine operations, the facility experienced an unexpected shut in by a third-party gas purchaser, causing sales gas to be routed to the HP flare. However, the sales gas did not ignite, even though the pilot was lit and properly positioned resulting in the venting of sales gas through the flare. Following the incident, SM conducted multiple investigations on the flare, and it was confirmed that all appropriate inspections and daily checks had been completed per SM protocol and the findings indicated no obvious cause for improper function. Additionally, attempts to replicate the scenario were unsuccessful, further suggesting that the flare was functioning as designed. The operations team is continuing to work with the flare manufacturer and field staff to determine if there are any other potential causal factors and solutions to mitigate the chances of a recurrence of this event.

cause: The Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) at Alon USA, LP - Big Spring Refinery (BSR) vented the reactor section to the South flare when the Wet Gas Compressor shut down. The shutdown occurred when the lube oil steam turbine pump failed, and the backup electrically driven pump failed to start. This led to the FCCU reducing feed rate and dropping reactor temperature to minimize flaring to the South Flare. During this event, the CO Boiler did not shut down and continued to process regenerator gases without impact. This event exceeded the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for SO2 > 500 lb/24hr at the South flare.
actions: Operations stabilized the FCCU by stopping charge and shuttering downstream process units immediately. Maintenance personnel began assessing the FCCU Wet Gas Compressor and lube oil pumps and discovered electrical circuit-breaker damage with no major compressor or pump damage. The circuit breaker internal components were replaced, and both the lube oil pump and Wet Gas Compressor were restarted. Once these were operational, the charge to the unit was restored and all flare activity returned to compliance.

cause: The Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) at Alon USA, LP - Big Spring Refinery (BSR) vented the regenerator section to the CO Boiler bypass stack when the #2 Air Blower shutdown. The shutdown occurred due to the intake air control valve positioner for the blower failing in the closed position. This led to immediate loss of air flow disrupting feed and catalyst movement, which led to the FCCU moving into a 'shutdown mode' that triggered the regenerator section to be routed to the bypass stack. This led to the FCCU reducing feed rate and dropping reactor temperature to minimize flaring to the South Flare. During this event, the CO Boiler did not shut down, however, all regenerator gases were routed to the bypass stack, as part of the safety systems. This led to exceeding the Reportable Quantity (RQ) limits for SO2 > 500 lb/24hr and CO > 5000 lb/24hr from the regenerator.
actions: Operations stabilized the FCCU by stopping charge and shuttering downstream process units immediately. Maintenance personnel began assessing the FCCU #2 Air Blower and discovered the faulty control valve positioner. The positioner was repaired and the components of the #2 Air Blower were inspected to ensure good operational status for restart. Once the blower was operational, the charge to the unit was restored and the regenerator section was routed back to the CO Boiler returning to compliance.

cause: The CO Boiler and FCCU underwent scheduled maintenance to water wash the CO Boiler superheater and reinstall the repaired #1 Blower. The CO Boiler was taken offline and bypassed to remove sodium fouling, while the blower installation restored normal FCCU operations. During the CO Boiler shutdown and dry-out, FCCU regenerator effluent was routed to the ESP bypass vent, and the reactor section vented to the South Flare. Emissions exceeded the SO₂ reportable quantity from the regenerator; CO and opacity remained below limits. South Flare emissions were within MSS permit limits.
actions: The FCCU charge was reduced to a safe minimum, and FCCU operations modified process conditions to reduce CO generation (full burn operations) prior to the CO Boiler shutdown and use of the bypass stack. In addition to operational changes to the FCCU, a CO Promoter (catalyst additive) was added, which reduced the CO pound-per-hour emissions by 90% while in the bypass stack. The work to install the FCCU #1 Blower occurred simultaneously with the CO Boiler tube water wash but required additional time to ensure its safe operation. During this additional time, the unit remained on circulation and regenerator discharge continued in the bypass stack while the boiler was in warm-up awaiting regenerator gas feed.
